4 · Shape control · Sec. 4

The map as a control reference

The time-consistent map closes the loop: two grippers deform a foam piece towards a target shape, with a deformation model that the controller learns from its own actions. The object is simulated with ARAP, as in the simulations of the paper (Sec. 4.2), and a depth camera above it delivers a new mesh at every iteration.

Shape error (Sec. 4)

The eigenbasis is invariant to isometries (a bent and a flat sheet can share it), so the error is extrinsic: the tracked points against their images on the target,

\begin{gathered}\E(k)=\X(k)-\Pi(k)\Y\\ \e(k)=[\e_1^\T(k),\dots,\e_M^\T(k)]^\T\in\R^{3M}\end{gathered}

Because \X(k) are the same object points at every frame, \Delta\x(k)=\x(k)-\x(k-1) is the motion of the object, and \Pi(k)\Y is a reference that does not jump.

Control law (Sec. 4.1)

The grippers act one at a time, so that every \Delta\x is the response to a single action \uv_g=(\Delta\mathbf t_g^\T,\Delta\mathbf r_g^\T)^\T (translation and Rodrigues vector). Each gripper keeps its last B actions \Um_g\in\R^{6\times B} and the responses \dX_g\in\R^{3M\times B}, which estimate its interaction matrix:

\Delta\x=\Lm_g\,\uv_g
\Lh_g=\dX_g\Um_g^\T\big(\Um_g\Um_g^\T+\gamma\I_6\big)^{-1}
\uv_g=-\alpha\,\Lh_g^{+}\,\e

For a good estimate, \Delta\e=\Delta\x=-\alpha\Lm_g\Lh_g^+\e=-\alpha\e: local exponential stability. The buffers start with B\ge 6 small exploratory actions of each gripper.

What the view shows

Colored sheetthe tracked mesh \X(k) (triangles of k=1), colored by \Pi(k) or by \|\e_m\|
Gray bodythe simulated object under the perceived surface
Orange ghostthe target mesh \Nc (points \Y)
Thin lineserror vectors from \x_m to \y_{\Pi(m)}
Violet dotsthe prediction \x+\Lh_g\uv_g of the controller's model for the next action, to compare with the next frame
Boxesgrippers g1 and g2; the one about to act is labeled

Try this

  1. Press Run with the T-shaped piece. The first iterations are the exploration: each gripper moves a little along each axis and back, to fill its buffers. Then the control law takes over and \|\e\| decreases, while \|\e_{\NTC}\|, computed from ZoomOut at every frame and never used by the controller, jumps as in Fig. 8.
  2. Turn on model prediction and use Step: the violet dots are where the model (22)–(23) expects the tracked points after the next action; the next frame shows where they went.
  3. Compare the two point-error distributions (Fig. 15): with the time-consistent map, the error of every point decreases smoothly; with ZoomOut at every frame, the distribution jumps from frame to frame.
  4. Lower \gamma to 10^{-6} and restart: as the actions shrink near the target, the responses \Delta\x are mostly sampling noise, the estimate (23) degrades, and the loop stalls. A Tikhonov term of the size of the actions keeps the estimate, and the loop, well conditioned.
  5. Choose the Mexican hat: as in the experiment of Fig. 10, only g2 moves; with one gripper the shape can still reach the target, which was produced the same way.

No model of the object is needed: the controller learns the local response of the object to each gripper from the tracked points, and this works only because the map is consistent in time. Deformable objects are under-actuated, and the error does not reach zero; here it settles near the scale of the sampling of the camera.

Implementation notes

Equation (23) is printed with -\gamma\I_6; as a Tikhonov regularization it adds \gamma\I_6, as here. In \Um_g, the rotations are multiplied by a lever of 10 cm (the displacement they produce at 10 cm from the gripper), so that a single \gamma weights translations and rotations alike; the control law (24) itself does not depend on this scaling. The paper does not give its values of \alpha, B, and \gamma; the defaults here are \alpha=0.15, B=24, \gamma=0.2\,\mathrm{cm}^2.

Every action is limited to 0.3 cm and 2.5° (the robots' step); with the small gain, the actions change smoothly from one iteration to the next. The exploration moves each gripper by 0.5 cm or 4° along each axis and back: more than a control step, so that the responses stand out from the sampling noise of the tracked points (about the size of a pixel); the buffer of 24 keeps them during the first 12 actions of each gripper. Targets are produced by the same ARAP simulator, by moving the grippers from the rest shape, so they are reachable; they are deformed about 1.35 times more than the targets of pages 1 and 2. The camera samples the top surface on a fixed pixel grid of about 1.1 cm with 0.5 mm of noise; the mapping uses the parameters of the reference code (\Ii=4, \Iu=5, \Imax=30, steps of 4) and the anchored tracking of page 2.
